title: Agentic system
summary: An agentic system, split into parts: 11 agents with separate roles, skills that load depending on the task, and gates where a person decides. It is how I work in my repos: the agents specify, build and review; merging, publishing and spending are mine to authorise.

facts.v: I designed it and maintain it; I approve every final gate
HandyX and Eclipse backends, Eclipse-Web and my own demos
For my own use: not open source

tldr.v: A general-purpose assistant on its own mixes scope, design, security and cost: it tends to assume, over-build and spend.
Roles with one owner per decision, discovery before code, written assumptions and gates with human approval.
In use in my repos, in a different shape in each one. The agents don't work on their own and nothing has been audited by a third party.

p: It is not a long prompt. Each agent is a Markdown file with its mission, what it decides, what it doesn't, and a table that says which skill to load for each action. Skills are short guides (one SKILL.md each, some with references) that load only when the task needs them.

I built it because a general-purpose assistant on its own mixes decisions about scope, design, security and cost. Here each decision has a single owner, discovery comes before code, assumptions are written down and there are gates where a person decides.
list: 11 agents: Direction, UX/UI, Design, Marketing, Ads, Documentation and five architects (frontend, backend, cybersecurity, games and trailers).
79 skills spread across 8 agents. Direction, UX/UI and Marketing have no skills of their own; UX/UI reuses some from Frontend and Trailers.
Three formats: Claude Code (all 11), Codex (10) and GitHub Copilot (5).

p: One owner per decision. UX/UI specifies flows and states, and Frontend implements them; Design signs off the aesthetics; Marketing decides offer and channel, and Ads makes the pieces; Backend implements and Cybersecurity reviews. Direction owns the plan, the scope and the cost, and hands each task to the right role.

diagram.title: Eleven agents, one owner per decision
diagram.caption: Under each role, its own skills (I counted the SKILL.md files on 10/28/2026). The arrows are hand-offs written in the agents' files or in the repos where they are used; Direction can hand work to any of them.

chief.label: Direction
chief.note: Writes and changes no code: decides scope, order and cost, and runs the gates.

design.label: Design
design.note: A 7-axis rubric and three written defects before accepting. If the result looks worse than the baseline, it is not merged.

fe.label: Frontend
fe.note: Whatever it needs from the backend it hands over as a requirement «to validate», never as something that already exists.

sec.label: Security
sec.note: Active tests only against our own dev or staging, with the scope written down. If the target is production or a third party, it stops and asks.

p: Every change follows the same path. No code without a bounded specification, one batch at a time, and nothing is merged or published without my OK.
Role agents load only the skills the action needs: a discovery one to start, layer or component ones to build, testing ones to close. If the review finds something blocking, it goes back to building.

diagram.title: From a request to production, through a human gate
diagram.caption: The G0–G5 labels are the gates of the working contract I use at Eclipse. At Eclipse the roles are steps that one session applies in sequence, with no parallel sub-agents.

spec.label: Specification
spec.note: Problem, user, flow, requirements and what is NOT done, acceptance criteria, how to roll back, cost and owner.

agents.label: Role agents
agents.note: Each one starts with its discovery skill and states its assumptions in a fixed block before implementing.

qa.label: QA
qa.note: Type check, lint, tests, build and captures at 360 and 1440 px; then another reviewer tries to refute each finding.

gate.label: Human gate
gate.note: Merging, deploying, spending, changing prices or publishing is my call, with an explicit, separate authorisation.

p: The gates and the levels come from the working contract I use at Eclipse; Direction's file defines the same six gates under other names. A gate is not passed with an empty title, an invented cost, a test that was not run or unlabelled fictional data, and a critical criterion worse than the baseline blocks even if the aesthetic score is high.
gates.title: Six gates, and who closes each one
gates.caption: The executor is the session that writes the code. Audiovisual production adds its own gates, from an approved storyboard to renders made in sequence.

steps.d: Do I know what I read and which version I'm working on?
Bounded scope, with exclusions and binary acceptance.
A comparable «before» and an exit test defined before changing anything.
Tests, type check, lint, build and captures at 360 and 1440 px, without touching production.
No critical criterion worse than the baseline.
An explicit, separate authorisation. No agent gives it.

p: Every claim carries its evidence level. Without evidence it is labelled «not tested» or «simulated», and what is proposed, implemented and tested are always kept apart. A batch is not «done» because a page exists: it goes from specified to verified locally, and I am the one who declares it «accepted».
evidence.title: Five evidence levels
evidence.caption: A real example: an Eclipse audit closes at E0 and E1 and states that the local test (E2) is still pending.

steps.d: I saw it in the code.
I verified it in a deployed environment.

p: The trailer QA skill reviews through six independent lenses: correctness and lifecycle, performance, accessibility, fidelity and honesty, premium level, and consistency with the repo.
Design uses a 7-axis rubric, scored 0 to 2, with binary blockers (focus, contrast, Back and Escape, reduced motion, honesty): a high score does not make up for a broken focus ring.
review.title: A finding has to survive
review.caption: From the trailer-qa skill. Security applies the same idea: it always tells a confirmed vulnerability apart from a suspicion.

steps.d: If it can't be reproduced or shown by reading the code, it is dropped.
Only what is blocking or high.
One table per lens and the real output of each command.

p: I checked it repo by repo on 10/28/2026. In each one the system takes a different shape, and in none of them does it work alone.

items.d: Three copied profiles (backend, cybersecurity and frontend) and 19 skills, identical byte for byte except the model line, with the source commit and the SHA-256 of each original. Two skills were left out on purpose; one because it models Sequelize and Prisma rules there. Backend implements, Cybersecurity reviews each phase's critical diff and Frontend reviews the contract, in sequence.

It follows the backend and cybersecurity profiles in Codex format. Its security review was done with isolated local tests, and it states that there were no third-party scans, real sends, deploys or migrations.
No agents are installed: the roles are steps that one session applies in sequence. What runs is the process: one owner per decision, the gates and the model policy.

Two e-commerce demos carry adapted copies of the frontend, games and trailer architects and the documentation agent (40 skills each), plus a project agent that delegates to them. The games demo carries frontend and games (21 skills).

p: They are written into the agents and apply to the work that comes out of them.

items.t: Security tests only on our own systems
items.d: Target, environment and isolation are written down before any active test. Findings carry file and line, severity, real impact and a concrete fix, framed by the OWASP Top 10, API Top 10 and ASVS.
Input validation, parameterised queries, every mutation in a transaction and errors without internal details.

items.t: Whatever has value is decided by the server
items.d: In games, the client reports an intent and the server decides the outcome.
No invented testimonials or metrics; anything fictional says «Demo»; text, prices and buttons live in HTML or SVG, never inside a generated video.
No spending, installing or publishing. A paid tool needs a dollar ceiling and my OK, and an external skill is installed only after checking its author, licence, SHA and scripts.

items.why: Each agent has its decision table and there is an ownership matrix. In the review's paper test, UX/UI was also «implementing» the header before the fix: two roles doing the same thing.

Backend, security, trailers and documentation start with their discovery skill, so nothing is built on wrong assumptions about routes, models, transactions or integrations. No silent decisions about language, folders, ORM or database.
Each agent loads the skill its table names for the concrete action. Context stays small, and Direction forbids reviewing everything before a localised task.

items.t: Sonnet by default, Opus with a reason
items.why: The larger model is used only at justified milestones, with its reason, deliverable and exit criterion recorded, and behind an aesthetic gate: if the result looks worse than the baseline, it is not merged. It comes from an earlier project with heavy Opus use and a poor aesthetic result.

items.t: Nothing in parallel without a budget
items.why: No parallel sub-agents or workers unless explicitly requested: one batch, one branch and one PR at a time.
items.alt: A panel of three creative directions in parallel, as one trailer skill asked for: at Eclipse they run in sequence.

items.why: Profiles reach each repo through a PR and a review, so existing rules are not overwritten. In HandyX each copy records its source commit and its SHA-256, and the only change is written down.

p: The agents repo is Markdown: it has no tests and no CI. Its test was a documentary review in Eclipse-Web of the first PR of the Eclipse agents, with the verdict «conditional adoption»; the corrections were applied afterwards.
What gets tested is the code this process produces: in the run of 10/27/2026, Eclipse-Web passed 463 tests, the Eclipse backend 779 and the internal portal 132, plus 14 complete browser journeys.

items.d: One folder and one definition file per role
In the review of the first Eclipse PR
Tested on paper, with and without the corrections

quality.note: On 10/28/2026 I counted the SKILL.md files in the Claude Code variants (69) plus the 10 in the documentation package: 79 files and 78 names, because project-analysis is in both Frontend and Documentation. The 11 agents, by folder and package.

list: It is not autonomous. Direction writes no code, and merging, deploying, spending, changing prices or publishing is my call.
They are not agents «installed» at Eclipse: there the roles are steps that one session runs in sequence.
It is not open source: the repo has no licence and is for my own use.
It is not an audit: the security agent can run a test against our own dev or staging, but no pentest has been done and there is no third-party review.

status.h: Status and what I don't claim
list: In use in my repos: 11 agents, 79 skills and three formats. The Eclipse agents came in through three PRs; the last one was merged on 10/26/2026.
Open: before installing them, I still need to check that Claude Code accepts the model alias and the header fields, and two trailer skills clash with the current flow.
The profiles declare different models depending on the tool; in HandyX that line was removed so they inherit the session's model.
The test figures belong to the repos the process produces, not to the agents repo.
I don't claim that the agents work on their own, that the system has been audited or that a pentest has been done.
